root.note: The Dutch word is certain as the source. Its own origin is unclear.

stages.meaning: the person who tells you what to do at work

history: Boss is an American word with Dutch roots. In the 1600s the Dutch founded New Amsterdam, today's New York. Their word baas meant ‘master, head of the house’. English speakers in the colonies took it over as boss. It became popular partly because many working people in America did not want to call anyone master, a word linked with servants and slaves. Boss sounded more equal. In the 1800s the word crossed the Atlantic to Britain. In some British cities, especially Liverpool, boss is also an informal adjective meaning ‘excellent’: That's boss! In Dutch, baasje, ‘little boss’, is the owner of a pet.
historyEinfach: Boss comes from Dutch. In the 1600s, Dutch people lived in New York. Their word baas meant ‘master’. Americans took the word. They did not like to say ‘master’, so they said boss. Later the word came to Britain.

synonyms.note: formal: the person or company that pays you

elsewhere.text: Dutch baas is still an everyday word for the person in charge at work. And when a dog walks with its owner, the owner is its baasje, its ‘little boss’.
